StaceviÄius / LRT Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius said the new government has no plans to raise taxes on businesses or households, despite removing a previous commitment from its program not to introduce new taxes during its term. Speaking after his first meeting with representatives of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists following the approval of the new cabinet, SinkeviÄius said the governmentâs intentions had not changed. âI cannot carve such a promise in stone, but there are no hidden intentions or plans to increase taxes,â the prime minister said. Instead, SinkeviÄius said the government intends to finance its social policy commitments through economic growth, moving funds and reallocating spending rather than by introducing new taxes. Vilnius central business district | V. Raupelis / LRT âWe will look for internal reserves to meet our social goals. That means some sectors will have to operate with less funding than before because priorities will be reviewed,â he said, without specifying which areas could face spending cuts. The new governmentâs program includes a range of social commitments, including financial incentives aimed at boosting the birth rate, changes to child benefits to help families maintain their income after the birth of a child, free meals for primary school pupils, higher funding for extracurricular education, increased pensions and measures to reduce poverty. Business leaders welcomed the prime ministerâs assurances but said they remained cautious about the policies of the centre-left government. âOf course, a left-wing government is a left-wing government, so those concerns exist,â said Vidmantas JanuleviÄius, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists. He said the business community had been reassured that social policy would not come at the expense of businesses. Vidmantas JanuleviÄius | P. Peleckis / BNS JanuleviÄius said the confederationâs long-term goal is for Lithuania to surpass Finland in gross domestic product per capita by 2035, arguing that achieving this would require greater investment in manufacturing and a stable tax environment. Opposition lawmaker Raimondas Kuodis of the conservative Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats questioned how the government would finance its promises, saying ministers had yet to provide clear answers. âThey donât appear to know themselves, [â¦] neither the finance minister nor the other social democratic luminaries,â he told LRT TV. âA triumph of the hope.â Economist EglÄ StonkutÄ of Vytautas Magnus University said Lithuania already faces pressure to keep its budget deficit within European Union limits, despite temporary flexibility for higher defence spending. She warned that the government would eventually need to address a growing fiscal gap, particularly after current defence-related exemptions expire, and said higher corporate taxes could become one option if policymakers seek additional revenue without alienating their voter base. âThe main two taxes generating most revenue are the value-added tax and the income tax,â she said. âThe social democrats will probably be reluctant to touch them.â Lithuania recently fell 13 places in a global competitiveness ranking, adding to concerns among businesses over the countryâs investment climate. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The Estonian government says it will shut the crossings after accusing Russia of directing an alleged sabotage attack on a drone manufacturer By Phoebe Hopson Published 16 November 2026 Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe". The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian. They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids. On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries. The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website. Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia". Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage. The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media. Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions. One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border. Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls." Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months. Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.
